# How EU Public Bodies Procure Solar Power: Tender Routes, Funding, Barriers and Data

## 1. How public bodies actually procure solar

**(A) Established facts.** Above the EU procurement thresholds, public bodies must advertise solar contracts on Tenders Electronic Daily (TED); the directives set the procedure menu. In practice, small and mid-sized solar projects for public buildings are overwhelmingly procured as **framework agreements** and **dynamic purchasing systems (DPS)** rather than one-off tenders. Examples: Portsmouth City Council's multi-contractor "Design, Supply & Installation Solar PV" framework (two lots up to £300k and £150k+, four years, ~£75m indicative) [12]; Kent County Council (trading as central purchasing body LASER Energy) running a five-lot framework covering supply, installation and even **power-purchase agreements (PPA) and "innovative funding"** [11]; and Gwynedd Council's 2020–2030 Energy & Sustainability Services DPS, open to authorities across England and Wales [13]. **Joint/cross-border procurement** is emerging: a Croatian project procured 36 PV plants (>1.5 MW total) on 21 public bodies' roofs (hospitals, schools, universities) through a single joint procedure, reporting significant price and staff-time savings [10].

**(B) Ongoing debate.** The EU Solar Energy Strategy and REPowerEU flag "aggregation" and "joint purchasing" as the intended future, but the Commission's own Big Buyers Working Together "Sustainable Solar" community still labels its PV procurement criteria and project guide as "concept"/draft documents that require national adaptation [9]. How widely DPS/framework routes have displaced one-off tenders is not systematically measured.

## 2. The role of EU funding

**(A) Established facts.** REPowerEU mobilised close to €300bn, with the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) "at the heart" of it; the Commission estimated ~€26bn of additional solar-PV investment (2022–2027) would be triggered [7][6]. The European Solar Rooftops Initiative, later hardened into the EU Solar Standard in the recast Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (2024), makes rooftop solar progressively mandatory on new public and commercial buildings (>250 m²) by 2026, renovated non-residential buildings by 2027, and existing public buildings by 2030 [6][16]. RRF-funded measures must pass a "do no significant harm" (DNSH) test per the Taxonomy Regulation, assessed measure-by-measure [4], and remain subject to EU **state-aid** rules (CEEAG, GBER, and the Temporary Crisis and Transition Framework) [5]. Public procurement rules apply in parallel where relevant [5].

**(B) Ongoing debate.** Whether member states' control systems actually guarantee that RRF solar spending complies with procurement and state-aid rules is contested: the European Court of Auditors concluded in 2025 that the Commission "has not been able to draw sufficient assurance" on this [3]. The precise share of RRF/Cohesion funding flowing to *public-body* (vs residential) solar is not authoritatively quantified.

## 3. Barriers and issues

**(A) Established facts.** The ECA's 2023 audit of EU procurement found that the 2014 reform had "no demonstrable effect" on several goals: contracting authorities and bidders still report **significant administrative burden**; SME participation has not markedly risen; and **strategic (green/social/innovative) criteria are rarely used** [2]. Lowest-price award still dominates — in eight member states over 80% of awards went to the lowest bid in 2021, a level the Commission's own Scoreboard red-flags [2]. OECD work catalogues regulatory and prequalification burdens that disproportionately hinder smaller actors in renewables [24].

**(B) Ongoing debate.** Whether aggregation genuinely reduces burden (as Croatia reports [10]) or simply shifts complexity to a lead buyer is debated; the US-oriented aggregation guides (RMI, WRI) stress pooling expertise but also the compliance cost of navigating incentive rules [3-search]. Quality-vs-price tension is an open, industry-contested question — SolarPower Europe is actively lobbying for "Made in Europe" sustainability/resilience criteria in public solar procurement, implying current price-driven awards disadvantage European manufacturing [23].

## 4. Demand-aggregation and joint-procurement initiatives

**(A) Established facts.** Three distinct models exist. (i) **Central purchasing bodies** run frameworks other authorities can call off from (LASER in England [11]). (ii) **Joint procurement** between public bodies (Croatia's 21-partner ACROSS procedure) [10]. (iii) **Collective-buying schemes** — the best-known is "Solar Together" (run by iChoosr, active in the UK/Netherlands/Belgium since 2013/2015, now ~15 UK regions a year), but it targets **households and small businesses, not public bodies' own assets** [14]. The Commission convenes the Big Buyers Working Together community to produce shared PV procurement criteria and guides, translated into 24 languages [9]; the Covenant of Mayors promotes "green public procurement" for locally generated renewable electricity [25].

**(B) Ongoing debate.** Whether these schemes "work" is contested. Solar Together has faced consumer complaints over installation delays [14], and its scope is residential — leaving a gap for public-sector aggregation, which remains dependent on ad-hoc CPB and JPP arrangements. There is no EU-wide, data-backed evaluation of public-sector solar aggregation outcomes.

## 5. Data quality and transparency

**(A) Established facts.** The ECA found TED data "not yet sufficiently complete and accurate": ~30% of contracts lack values (broadly unchanged since 2017), ~86% lack national registration numbers, ~63% lack estimated award value, and there is **no common EU-wide supplier identifier**, blocking cross-border and beneficial-ownership analysis [2]. The **below-threshold gap** is structural: only above-threshold notices *must* be published on TED, while below-threshold municipal contracts are scattered across national portals in incompatible formats — the Commission itself calls this the core motivation for the **Public Procurement Data Space (PPDS)**, launched 24 September 2024 [1]. The PPDS and the **eForms** migration are intended to add structured, optional fields on green/social/innovative procurement and to monitor data quality [1][20].

**(B) Ongoing debate.** Academics and think-tanks argue the tools still fall short: Telles critiques the PPDS/eForms design and the "lost decade" of e-procurement [20]; Bruegel notes "vastly different coverage" across sources, thin green-procurement data and "databases of limited quality" [17]; ENTSO-E (2026) and a 2026 Publications Office assessment both stress that major weaknesses persist in completeness, lifecycle coverage, interoperability and accountability [18][19]. BridgeGap researchers describe having to hunt for "suitable" procurement data to fight corruption [19]. Whether optional eForms fields will actually be populated is an open question the Commission itself flags [2].

## 6. Existing benchmarks and studies

**(A) Established facts.** General EU procurement benchmarks exist — a World Bank study analysed ~3.6 million TED contract awards (2018–2023) [22] — and academic work (Tátrai 2024) stresses that TED can only be analysed "after comprehensive data cleaning" [21]. TED publishes 700,000+ notices annually [21].

**(B) Open question / gap.** I found **no authoritative, dedicated quantification of *public-sector solar* procurement in the EU** (no reliable count, total value, or country breakdown for solar-specific CPV codes such as 09330000/09331000/09331200). This is a genuine evidence gap — and a possible benchmark your TED dataset could help fill, provided you flag the same caveats the ECA raised about value completeness and below-threshold under-coverage.

# EU public procurement of solar power: policy framework and debates

*Access date for all sources: 2026-11-25. (A) = established fact; (B) = contested/debated position.*

## 1. EU Solar Energy Strategy and the Rooftops Initiative

(A) The **EU Solar Energy Strategy** (COM(2022) 221, 18 May 2022) set targets of more than **320 GW of solar PV by 2025** (surpassed) and **almost 600 GW by 2030**; the Commission now cites a 2030 target of at least 700 GW. [1] Its flagship, the **European Solar Rooftops Initiative**, proposed making rooftop solar compulsory for all new public and commercial buildings over 250 m² (by 2026), existing public and commercial buildings over 250 m² (by 2027), and new residential buildings (by 2029). [1]

(A) These obligations were legislated through the recast **Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD, 2024)**, Article 10, which requires new buildings to be "solar-ready" and existing public buildings to install solar "where technically, economically and functionally feasible", phased by size: above 2,000 m² from 1 January 2028, above 750 m² from 2029, and above 250 m² from 2031 (schools, hospitals, administration buildings). [2] This is the main legal driver of solar demand by public bodies, complementing the TED procurement pipeline.

## 2. Net-Zero Industry Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1735)

(A) The **NZIA** entered into force on 29 June 2024. It sets a 2030 target of domestic manufacturing capacity covering 40% of EU deployment needs, and applies to solar PV among 12+ net-zero technologies. [3][4] For **public procurement, Article 25** imposes three kinds of requirements on contracting authorities [3][4][5]:

1. **Minimum mandatory environmental sustainability requirements** (Art 25(1)) — set by implementing act, applicable from **30 June 2026**. The act adopted — **Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/718** of 20 March 2026 — in practice covers **wind-turbine-blade recyclability**; PV-specific carbon-footprint minimums were not yet set, a gap flagged by industry. [5][6][7]
2. **At least one additional non-price requirement** (Art 25(3)) — for works contracts/concessions, chosen among: a social/employment condition, **cybersecurity compliance**, or a **timely-delivery obligation**. Applied immediately from June 2024. [4][5]
3. **A resilience contribution** (Art 25(7)) — requiring diversification where the EU is highly dependent on a single third country, applicable from **30 December 2025**, operationalised by **Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1178** (list of final products and main specific components) and a Commission Communication on shares of Union supply (23 May 2025). [8][9]

(A) The resilience trigger: more than 50% of EU supply of a final product from a single third country (or 40% rising by ≥10 pp over two years). For **PV cells the threshold is >85% from a single country** — i.e. China — which activates the diversification test for modules/cells/inverters. [5][8] The Art 25 guidance (Communication C/2026/4623, OJ 31.8.2026) sets reference values (e.g. PV modules ≈26.6%, cells ≈20.4%, inverters ≈20.4% of hardware cost) and GPA carve-outs. [5]

(A) **Article 26** governs renewable-energy **auctions** (distinct from classic procurement): mandatory pre-qualification criteria (responsible business conduct, cybersecurity/data security, ability to deliver) plus sustainability/resilience criteria, applying to at least **30% of auctioned volume per year (or 6 GW)**, with a combined **15–30% weighting** (minimum 5% per criterion), detailed in **Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1176**. [3][9][10] Non-binding guidance for both Articles was published on 22 July 2026. [10]

## 3. European Solar Charter (15 April 2024)

(A) The **European Solar Charter**, signed 15 April 2024 by the Commission, **23 Member States and ~100 companies**, is a voluntary instrument committing signatories to early implementation of NZIA non-price criteria (resilience, sustainability, responsible business conduct, "ability to deliver", innovation, cybersecurity) in both **renewable auctions and public procurement**, plus demand-aggregation and a **"Community of Public Buyers for Sustainable Solar PV"**. [11][12] (A) It contains **no trade-defence measures**, owing to lack of consensus. [13] (A) The Commission reports a 2026 progress review, EIB co-financing (e.g. €560m for 3SUN), and Innovation Fund support (€445m to solar manufacturing). [11][14]

## 4. Debates and controversies

**(a) Thresholds and weighting.** (B) Industry diverges on how far non-price criteria (NPCs) should bite. SolarPower Europe urges applying **resilience as an award (not pre-qualification) criterion**, keeping the 15–30% weighting band, and prioritising carbon footprint. [10][15] By contrast, **BDEW** (German energy/water association) warns the criteria are "very complex", create bureaucracy, lengthen processing times and could reverse achieved permitting acceleration. [16] **Green Power Denmark** calls the secondary legislation "very complex and difficult to understand", risking "27 different national approaches". [17]

**(b) Cheapest panels vs resilience/security.** (A) The NZIA's stated aim is to shift procurement "away from lowest price" toward sustainability/resilience. [3][9] (B) Critics (BDEW, Green Power Denmark) argue any cost premium for European products raises system costs, in tension with lowering energy prices. [16][17] (A) On implementation, only **six Member States** had applied NZIA solar rules by October 2026 — Italy furthest, awarding **1.1 GW** (FER-X) excluding Chinese cells/modules/inverters; Austria, France, Ireland, Lithuania and Spain took divergent routes. [18]

**(c) Cybersecurity.** (A) Inverters are the recognised control-point vulnerability. [19] (B) The Commission's Smart Energy Expert Group notes the current NZIA implementing act "only covers a small fraction of PV installations" and bidders "only need to prepare a cybersecurity plan", so it "does not allow to restrict the use of high-risk suppliers"; it looks to the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) to exclude high-risk suppliers under the revised Cybersecurity Act. [20] SolarPower Europe seeks NIS2/CRA-aligned standards for inverters. [21]

**(d) "Buy European" vs single market/WTO.** (B) This is the sharpest tension. The NZIA's resilience criterion and the IAA's "Made in EU" origin requirements "clash with the longstanding prohibition… of local-content requirements", consistent with WTO GPA commitments. [22] CEPS concludes the EU has built an "origin preference regime" "inadvertently", instrument by instrument, with local-content thresholds "directly in tension with GPA Article IV(1)". [23] The IAA attempts mitigation by treating GPA/FTA-partner content as EU-equivalent. [22][23]

**(e) Cost and pace.** (B) Contested. The Jacques Delors Centre argues stronger Buy-European/low-carbon rules "need not break the bank" and that the NZIA's 15% cost escape clause (IAA proposes raising to 20%) should be retained to shield energy prices. [24] SolarPower Europe warns "Made in EU" must not undermine electrification, given electrification's CAPEX intensity. [21]

**(f) Legal challenges and industry criticism.** (A) No formal annulment challenge is yet documented; criticism is concentrated in position papers. (B) German industry leaders reportedly denounced the IAA as a "bureaucratic monster" (Politico, cited in [22]); BDEW and Green Power Denmark raise proportionality and single-market fragmentation concerns. [16][17] The IAA proposal (4 March 2026) is politically contested between industrial Member States and "end-consumer" Member States facing higher costs. [25]

## 5. Adjacent policy

(A) **REPowerEU** (2022) is the parent plan of the Solar Strategy. [1] (A) The **Critical Raw Materials Act** (Regulation (EU) 2024/1252, in force 23 May 2024) sets 2030 benchmarks (10% extraction, 40% processing, 25% recycling; ≤65% from any single country) and underpins solar-component security-of-supply logic, reinforced by the RESourceEU Action Plan (Dec 2025). [26] (A) The **Clean Industrial Deal** (26 Feb 2025) announced >€100bn for EU clean manufacturing, a 2026 review of the Public Procurement Directives to add sustainability/resilience/"European preference" criteria, the **Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework** (CISAF, 25 June 2025) for solar-manufacturing aid, and the **Industrial Accelerator Act** (proposed March 2026) with "Made in EU" procurement rules. [27][28][29]

---

# EU public procurement of solar PV: the supply-chain and trade dimension

## 1. The scale of Chinese dominance in the EU solar-PV supply chain

**(A) Established facts.** China's share of every major solar-PV manufacturing stage exceeds 80%, and is highest upstream. The IEA's flagship *Solar PV Global Supply Chains* report (2022, data updated 2024) puts China above 80% across polysilicon, ingots, wafers, cells and modules; its *Advancing Clean Technology Manufacturing* (2024) reports China holds more than 80% of global module manufacturing capacity and 95% of wafer capacity. IEA-PVPS data show China's share of global polysilicon production rising from 86% (2022) to 92% (2023) and 94% (2024). On the demand side, the European Solar Manufacturing Council (ESMC) states China accounted for more than 95% of the EU's solar-panel imports by value in 2024; Bruegel cites the same >95% figure for 2022. By contrast, the IEA puts Europe's share of global PV manufacturing at roughly 1%.

Inverters are the partial exception: Europe retains significant domestic players (SMA, Fronius), but Chinese vendors dominate globally — Huawei and Sungrow held about 55% of the global inverter market in 2024 (Wood Mackenzie), and nine of the world's top ten inverter vendors are Chinese. SMA announced a restructuring of up to 1,100 jobs in November 2024.

## 2. Trade-defence posture: 2013–2018 measures and 2023–2026 developments

**(A) Established facts.** In December 2013 the EU imposed anti-dumping (AD) and anti-subsidy/countervailing (ASD/CVD) duties on Chinese solar cells and modules, using a minimum import price (MIP) plus a volume undertaking. Bruegel estimates the measures raised Chinese panel prices in Europe by an average of ~47% from August 2013. The measures were extended 18 months in March 2017 and lapsed on 3 September 2018 (confirmed in a European Parliament written answer).

The one live trade-defence dossier in the sector concerns **solar glass**, not panels. Following an expiry review opened in July 2025, the Commission repealed the AD duty (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2314) and the countervailing duty (Regulation (EU) 2026/2310) on Chinese solar glass on 21–22 October 2026, after more than 12 years. The Commission's stated reason is that "no Union industry exists" — the last two EU producers, GMB and AGC Glass Europe, had left the market.

**(B) Debated / contested.** There has been **no formal initiation** of a new AD/CVD investigation into Chinese modules or cells in 2023–2026. In 2025 ESMC, joined by 23 European PV organisations, publicly demanded stricter import controls and new trade-defence tools, claiming Chinese TOPCon modules are sold in Europe at €0.109/Wp — about 31% below the €0.159/Wp ESMC says is needed to cover production and shipping (a ~46% "dumping margin"). The Commission has signalled it does not intend to impose trade restrictions on solar, and Germany has separately been reported to be weighing national barriers. These are proposals and signals, not enacted measures.

## 3. The Foreign Subsidies Regulation (FSR) and public procurement

**(A) Established facts.** The FSR (Regulation (EU) 2022/2560) applies since 12 July 2023, with mandatory notification in public procurement since 12 October 2023. Bidders must notify foreign financial contributions (FFCs) where the contract is worth at least €250 million and the bidder received at least €4 million in FFCs per non-EU country over the prior three years.

The first-ever FSR in-depth investigation (February 2024) targeted Chinese state-owned train-maker CRRC in a Bulgarian tender; CRRC withdrew. The solar sector followed: on 3 April 2024 the Commission opened two in-depth investigations into Chinese bidders for the 454.97 MW Rovinari photovoltaic park in Romania (partly financed by the EU Modernisation Fund) — the LONGi Solar Technologie/ENEVO consortium and two Shanghai Electric entities. Both withdrew in May 2024, and the Commission closed the probes without imposing remedies. Separately, in April 2024 the Commission opened its first *ex officio* FSR investigation, into Chinese wind-turbine suppliers.

**(B) Assessment / debate.** No FSR duties have yet been imposed in solar; the instrument's effect has been deterrent — Chinese bidders withdrew rather than face scrutiny. Analysts (Cleary, Taylor Wessing, Stibbe) read this as proof the FSR is reshaping Chinese participation in large EU tenders, though some argue it has yet to deliver substantive remedies. The China Chamber of Commerce to the EU criticised the probes as introducing uncertainty into tenders.

## 4. The European Solar Charter and the "Made in Europe" procurement debate

**(A) Established facts.** The European Solar Charter was signed on 15 April 2024 by 23 EU member states, the Commission and industry. It commits signatories to voluntary actions: accelerated permitting for manufacturing and deployment, "ambitious non-price criteria" in public procurement and renewable-energy auctions, and access to EU funding (Recovery and Resilience Facility, Innovation Fund). It is explicitly framed as early implementation of the Net-Zero Industry Act (NZIA).

The NZIA (in force since June 2024) sets a benchmark that EU manufacturing meet 40% of annual deployment needs by 2030, and the European Solar PV Industry Alliance (ESIA) targets 30 GW of manufacturing capacity across the value chain by 2030 (requiring ~€30bn investment, per SolarPower Europe). From 30 December 2025, an NZIA implementing act requires member states to apply non-price criteria (sustainability and resilience) to at least 30% of annual renewable-auction volume (or 6 GW); the Commission published guidance in July 2026.

**(B) Debated.** The Charter stops short of quotas or explicit price preferences for EU-made modules, relying instead on "non-price" resilience criteria — a deliberate compromise. ESMC and manufacturers argue these are too weak and slow to compete with Chinese pricing; SolarPower Europe and deployment-focused firms warn that mandatory "Made in Europe" shares or tariffs would slow the energy transition and raise costs for public bodies and consumers.

## 5. The central tension: cheap imports vs strategic autonomy

**(A) The conflict.** Chinese panels are dramatically cheaper, letting public bodies and taxpayers decarbonise faster. ESMC's own figures illustrate the gap: imported Chinese modules at €0.109/Wp versus an estimated €0.159/Wp sustainable European price. Reshoring therefore means materially higher procurement costs and slower deployment.

**(B) Actor positions (attributed).**
- **Manufacturers (ESMC, Meyer Burger):** demand trade defence, "resilience" procurement preferences, and forced-labour-linked import controls to level the playing field.
- **SolarPower Europe (broad value chain, incl. installers/EPCs):** explicitly opposes trade-defence measures ("There must be no trade defence measures on solar PV products entering Europe", echoed by 420+ organisations under #MakeSolarEU), but endorses non-price resilience criteria and "European preference provisions where appropriate for strategic sectors".
- **European Commission:** has signalled no appetite for new solar trade restrictions, favouring the FSR and non-price criteria.
- **Member states:** split — Germany has floated national trade barriers; others prioritise cheap deployment.
- **NGOs / human-rights groups:** focus on forced labour in Xinjiang polysilicon rather than prices; the EU Forced Labour Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/3015, applying from 14 December 2027) will ban products linked to forced labour, with polysilicon seen as the highest-risk input.
- **Trade unions:** support local manufacturing to protect jobs.

The core disagreement is whether resilience is best served by restricting imports (risk of higher prices and retaliation) or by demand-side support and diversification (Slower, costlier build-out of EU capacity).

## 6. Key data points: capacity vs demand, closures, NZIA/ESIA targets

**(A) Established facts.**
- **Demand:** the EU installed a record ~65.5 GW in 2024; SolarPower Europe projects ~65.1 GW in 2025 — the first market contraction in nearly a decade.
- **Supply:** Europe holds only ~1% of global PV manufacturing capacity (IEA), far below demand; the gap is met almost entirely by Chinese imports.
- **Factory closures:** Meyer Burger announced closure of its Freiberg, Germany module plant in early 2024 and a pivot to the US, then reversed course in August 2024 (cancelling a Colorado cell plant); its German subsidiaries filed for insolvency in 2025, and its US arm filed for Chapter 11 in June 2025 — widely cited as the emblematic failure of European PV manufacturing under Chinese price pressure. In solar glass, the last two EU producers (GMB, AGC Glass Europe) exited, prompting the 2026 duty repeal.
- **Targets:** NZIA 40% of deployment needs and ESIA's 30 GW manufacturing capacity by 2030.

**(B) Contested.** Analysts dispute whether the 30 GW/40% goals are achievable — Bruegel and others note that even if all announced projects materialise, Europe's cost disadvantage persists, and SolarPower Europe warns industrial-policy roll-out has been too slow to reverse factory closures.

Research is complete and compiled into `docs/agent-notes/`. Here's the surfaced picture of **issues and ongoing debates** around public tenders for solar power in the EU.

## What I found (three parallel sub-agents)

**The demand side is being engineered.** Public bodies are being pushed to buy solar through the EPBD "EU Solar Standard" (rooftop solar on existing public buildings by 2028–2031), REPowerEU / Recovery & Resilience funding, and open tenders. Our own data reflects this: 60.9% of awards are EU-funded, 82.6% open procedure.

**But the rules for *how* they buy are being rewritten** by the Net-Zero Industry Act (Reg. 2024/1735), Art. 25, which now layers onto public tenders: environmental-sustainability minimums, at least one non-price requirement (cybersecurity / social / delivery), and a **resilience/diversification criterion** triggered because >85% of PV-cell supply comes from one country (China).

## The five live debates

1. **Non-price criteria vs "cheapest panel"** — SolarPower Europe wants resilience as an award criterion; BDEW/Green Power Denmark call it bureaucratic and risk 27 divergent national regimes. Only **six member states** were applying the rules by Oct 2026.
2. **"Made in Europe" vs single market / WTO-GPA** — CEPS argues the EU has built an origin-preference regime "inadvertently", in direct tension with GPA's ban on local-content conditions (sharpened by the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act).
3. **Cheap imports vs strategic autonomy (China)** — China holds >80% of every PV stage and >95% of EU panel imports; the 2018 duties lapsed, no new module duties, but the **Foreign Subsidies Regulation** drove Chinese bidders out of Romania's Rovinari tender. Industry is split: manufacturers want trade defence; SolarPower Europe + 420 orgs oppose it.
4. **Cybersecurity** — inverters (Huawei/Sungrow ≈55% of the market) are the control-point risk; current rules can't exclude high-risk suppliers.
5. **Cost & pace** — resilience/"Buy European" rules risk raising prices for public bodies and slowing electrification.

**Plus a data issue relevant to our project:** the ECA found ~30% of TED contracts lack values, there's no common supplier identifier, and below-threshold municipal contracts are structurally under-covered — and **no solar-specific quantification of EU public procurement exists at all**, which is a gap our dataset could help fill.
